t: Cat and Mouse II — Minimax on a Tiny Board
o:
This is a two-player perfect-information game on a board of at most 8 × 8 cells. Mouse moves first, then the players alternate single jumps: up to their jump limit along one straight direction, stopping at walls or the border; staying put is a legal move, and Mouse may jump over Cat. Cat wins by catching Mouse or reaching the food first; Mouse wins by reaching the food first; and if the chase drags past 1000 turns without resolution, the rules hand the win to Cat.
Because both sides play optimally, we evaluate the game tree over states (mouse cell, cat cell, whose turn). A state is a Mouse-win exactly when the mover can force it: Mouse needs at least one move leading to a Mouse-win state; Cat needs all of its moves to lead there. The board is so small that memoizing every state — including a move counter used to cut off hopeless chases — runs in milliseconds.
Example 1 ("####F" / "#C..." / "M...."): whatever square the Cat threatens, the Mouse keeps distance and darts to F first → true. Examples 2–3 use "M.C...F": with mouseJump = 4 the Mouse outruns the Cat to F (true); with mouseJump = 3 the Cat controls the corridor and wins (false).
k: Model the game as minimax over states (mouse position, cat position, turn parity): Mouse maximizes, Cat minimizes.
A repeated state means looping play, so capping the ply count at twice the number of cells safely detects chases the Mouse cannot force — and draws belong to the Cat by rule.
Precompute each floor cell’s reachable set once per jumper: walls terminate only their own direction, never the whole move.
Terminal checks have priority: being caught outranks food, and whoever steps onto the food ends the game immediately.

a.n: Approach 1: Memoized Minimax with a Move Cap
a.i: Depth-first evaluation memoized on (mouse, cat, plies elapsed). At each state settle the terminals first: Mouse on food is an immediate Mouse-win; sharing a cell or Cat on food is a Cat-win; once the counter passes a cap of 2·rows·cols plies declare a Cat-win — sound because any genuinely winning plan can avoid repeating a state, and there are at most 2·(rows·cols) distinct states. Then expand the mover’s options with any/all semantics: Mouse wants one winning child, Cat wants at least one child where the Mouse loses.
s: Locate M, C, F; encode cells as integers; precompute move lists for both animals (stay plus each direction up to the jump limit, breaking at walls).
dfs(m, c, t) returns whether the Mouse wins from that state; memoize results.
Apply terminal rules, then branch over the current mover’s list: any for Mouse turns, all for Cat turns.
a.t: O(T · S^2 · D) worst case — S = rows·cols ≤ 64 cells, T = 2S capped plies, D = average move-list length; a few million steps at 8×8.
a.sp: O(T · S^2) for the memo table.

a.n: Approach 2: Retrograde Analysis (BFS from Terminal States)
a.i: Instead of top-down recursion, classify every state bottom-up — enumerating pairs of floor cells only, since neither player can ever stand on a wall (wall-occupant phantom states would corrupt degree counts). Seed all terminal states (Mouse at food ⇒ Mouse-win; shared cell or Cat at food ⇒ Cat-win) into a queue, and give every undecided state a degree equal to its mover’s number of moves. Popping a decided state s informs each parent — a state from which the previous mover stepped into s: if s favors that mover, the parent is decided immediately in their favor; otherwise the parent loses one escape route, and when no routes remain it adopts s’s outcome. States left unresolved participate only in infinite chases — draws, which the rules award to the Cat.
s: Precompute move lists per jumper; enumerate states (mouse, cat, turn) over floor-cell pairs only.
Mark terminal states and queue them; set degree = mover’s move-list size for every other state.
Pop a decided state s and enumerate parents by undoing one move of the previous mover.
If s’s winner equals the previous mover, decide the parent identically and queue it; otherwise decrement its degree, deciding it against the mover when the degree reaches zero.
Return true iff the start state ended up Mouse-win (unresolved counts as a Cat win).
a.t: O(S^2 · D) — every state’s incoming moves are scanned a constant number of times (D ≈ average move-list length); tiny at 8×8.
a.sp: O(S^2) for the result and degree arrays.

w: Open with the memoized minimax — it mirrors how people naturally reason about games — then present retrograde analysis as the polished version with guaranteed bounds and no recursion-depth concerns. Classic bugs: letting jumps slide through walls (must break per direction), forgetting that staying put is legal, checking food before capture (capture outranks), mishandling draws (they are Cat wins, which is precisely why a move cap is legitimate — justify it via the pigeonhole argument on repeated states), and evaluating phantom states on wall cells during bottom-up passes (they silently corrupt degree counts). Edge cases: Mouse starting adjacent to Cat, food reachable in one hop, and jump lengths larger than the board. Follow-ups: also output the number of turns under optimal play (store distances instead of booleans), add a third player, or forbid jumping over the Cat.
